clue.text: Have great success as bowler may do, and put cap back on

parts.note: in the game of bowls a player aims to strike the jack, the small target ball

indicators.note: back tells us to read the word for cap from right to left

parts.note: a cap or lid is the top of something

explanation.surface: A bowls player strikes lucky and celebrates by putting a cap back on.
explanation.walkthrough: In bowls (lawn bowling) the jack is the small white target ball. 'back' turns TOP into POT, which goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To win the top prize of a gamble is an idiom for enjoying sudden great success.

clue.text: They gamble recklessly to make level required in exams

indicators.note: one thing required in another sits inside it, so the levelling word goes into the exams

parts.note: Highers are the Scottish school-leaving examinations
to roll a lawn or road is to flatten it with a roller

explanation.surface: Students needing top grades take wild chances in their exams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'level' looks like a school grade, but the verb phrase means flatten, as a garden roller does; Highers are exams sat by Scottish pupils at about seventeen.
explanation.definitionFit: Big-staking gamblers who bet heavily are called by this name, a casino idiom.

clue.text: Lock requiring pressure, failing to open

indicators.note: a word failing to open has lost its first letter

parts.note: stress is pressure or strain

explanation.surface: A lock that needs force to work will not open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failing to open' removes the first S of STRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: A tress is a lock of hair, a long curl or strand.

clue.text: Buzz about Elvis Presley's second unusual appearance in European city

indicators.note: one word put about another surrounds it, so the buzz wraps the rest

parts.note: a hum is a low buzzing sound

indicators.note: unusual means the letters are set out in a strange new order
second points to the second letter of the singer's surname

explanation.surface: Excitement surrounds a strange Elvis sighting in a continental city.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second letter of the singer's surname joins the shuffle; Elvis sightings are a running joke about his 'unusual appearance', which disguises the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilversum is a Dutch city, known as the home of the Netherlands' broadcasting.

clue.text: Mandible of rabbit, black one

parts.note: to rabbit or jaw is British slang for chattering on
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: An anatomist examines the jaw of a black rabbit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rabbit' looks like the animal, but in British slang to rabbit (on) means to talk at length, as does to jaw.
explanation.definitionFit: The mandible is the lower jaw bone in anatomy, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Bar in residential street

definitions.meaning: to bar a road or door is to shut it off
a cul-de-sac or short street of houses is often named this in Britain

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means shut or block; as a British noun it is a quiet dead-end street of homes.

clue.text: Headmaster's guiding theory 'given in report

indicators.note: a report here is something heard, so the word is spoken and its sound kept

parts.note: a principle is a fundamental rule or theory that guides conduct

explanation.surface: A school head sets out his educational philosophy in a written report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'report' seems to be a school report, but signals speech: PRINCIPLE said out loud matches the other spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of a school or college is called its principal, especially in American and Scottish usage.

clue.text: Slug, a little one

definitions.meaning: a slug is a gulp or small measure of spirits

explanation.definitionFit: It is both a small dram of whisky and a word for a very young child.

clue.text: Faint when not very fit and shivering

indicators.note: not says the letter for very is left out

parts.note: a faint idea is a vague one

explanation.surface: Someone feels faint when out of shape and starts to shiver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when not very' takes V from VAGUE; 'fit' looks like healthy but means an attack of illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Ague is an old name for malarial fever, marked by bouts of shaking chills.

clue.text: Professional body is a costly one we' fancy

indicators.note: fancy as a verb means imagine, so the letters are reimagined in a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A trade association is pricey, one we might quite like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' shuffles A, COSTLY, I and WE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Law Society is the body that represents solicitors in England and Wales.

clue.text: Get on well with old duke

parts.note: to prosper is to thrive or do well

explanation.surface: An elderly aristocrat gets along nicely with everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: Prospero is the deposed Duke of Milan in Shakespeare's The Tempest.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's magician in The Tempest is a dispossessed duke, so the name is an example.

clue.text: Old copper's given directions out ri

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
S and E are compass points, south and east

explanation.surface: A retired policeman is given instructions to get out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a police officer, but is the metal, Cu.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretext offers a way out of an obligation, so an alibi-like noun can be called an out.

clue.text: Arrange' escape of 8, causing excitement at start of March

parts.note: to spring a prisoner is to free him from jail
8 across is a fever, so the cross-reference gives fever

explanation.surface: Organising a jailbreak for a sick man stirs up thrills as March begins.
explanation.walkthrough: '8' refers to the answer of 8 across, the shivering illness, for which a synonym is used.
explanation.definitionFit: The restless excitement felt when spring arrives, which begins in March, has this idiomatic name.

clue.text: Person in disgrace taking stock behind bar?

indicators.note: behind places the stock after the word for bar

parts.note: to black goods or a firm is to boycott or bar them, in trade-union usage
sheep are livestock

explanation.surface: Someone disgraced is drinking in the back of a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stock' and 'bar' suggest a pub's supplies, but are livestock and a union boycott.
explanation.definitionFit: The disreputable member of a family is idiomatically called this, a dark animal among a white flock.

clue.text: Clubs, dance hall and restaurant

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
a hop is an informal dance
a house is a hall for public entertainment, like an opera house

explanation.surface: A night out takes in nightclubs, a dance hall and a restaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: A chophouse is a restaurant specialising in steaks and chops.

clue.text: - Wonders about name on bottom of mobile phone

indicators.note: in a down answer, a piece on the bottom of another comes after it
mobile means moving, so the letters of phone move around
about here means in a jumbled order, so the letters of name are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone marvels at finding a name written on the underside of a mobile phone.
explanation.walkthrough: Two anagrams, each with its own signal: 'mobile' looks like part of the phrase mobile phone, and in a down entry 'on bottom of' means placed below.
explanation.definitionFit: Phenomena are remarkable events or marvels, so wonders is a synonym.

clue.text: No end of privilege, attending university in the country

indicators.note: no end of means the final letter is lost

parts.note: a perk is a perquisite or privilege of a job

explanation.surface: Endless privilege comes with going to university in a country seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of' drops K from PERK.
explanation.definitionFit: Peru is a South American country, so it is one instance of a nation.

clue.text: Love someone extremely unimportant

definitions.meaning: love is the score of nothing in tennis

explanation.definitionFit: It is the tennis nil score and a word for a person of no importance.

clue.text: I'm singularly bound to include what various authors contribute

definitions.text: I'm singularly bound to include what various authors contribute

parts.words: I'm singularly bound to include what various authors contribute
parts.note: the book speaks: a single bound volume gathering together pieces by many different writers

explanation.surface: Someone tied up alone has to take in the work of many writers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound' seems to mean obliged, but describes a book's binding, and 'singularly' means as one volume.
explanation.definitionFit: An anthology collecting assorted writings is a miscellany, a varied collection.

clue.text: Riff-raff seize posh Conservative then British give in

indicators.note: to seize is to hold, so the riff-raff word grips the next pieces inside it

parts.note: scum is the dregs of society, riff-raff
U means upper-class, posh

explanation.surface: A mob grabs a Tory toff, and the British surrender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seize' puts UC inside SCUM, then B follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To succumb is to yield or surrender, a straight synonym of give in.

clue.text: Avoid nearly all Dutch artist's work at first

indicators.note: nearly all keeps everything but the final letter

parts.note: M. C. Escher was a Dutch graphic artist

indicators.note: at first takes the opening letter of work

explanation.surface: Steer clear of almost every early work by a Dutch painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly all' trims R from ESCHER; 'at first' gives W.
explanation.definitionFit: To eschew something is to shun or abstain from it, a formal synonym.

clue.text: Enquiry about drug: grass?

indicators.note: about puts the question word round the drug

parts.note: what? is a word of enquiry
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Someone asks about drugs: is it cannabis?
explanation.walkthrough: 'grass' looks like marijuana but is the cereal plant; the question mark flags an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheat is a cereal and a member of the grass family, so grass is defined by example.

clue.text: Leave factory, unwell after hit on head

indicators.note: unwell comes after hit, so its word follows

parts.note: to clock someone is slang for hitting them, often on the head
off means slightly ill, feeling off

explanation.surface: A worker goes home sick after a blow to the head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit on head' is British slang, to clock someone; 'unwell' as off is also British, as in feeling a bit off.
explanation.definitionFit: Workers clock off when they finish a shift and leave the workplace, a phrasal verb.

clue.text: Out East, snake capsized boat one time

indicators.note: capsized means turned upside down, so in a down clue the boat word reads upwards

parts.note: Noah's ark is a boat
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: In Asia, a snake overturns a boat once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capsized' turns ARK into KRA.
explanation.definitionFit: The krait is a venomous snake found in South and Southeast Asia, hence out East.

clue.text: Unique diet, bananas, that brings anxiety

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

explanation.surface: A peculiar diet of bananas leaves someone worried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' looks like the fruit in the diet, but is slang for mad and shuffles UNIQUE DIET.
explanation.definitionFit: Inquietude is restlessness or unease of mind, a formal synonym.

clue.text: Trouble for a horse

definitions.meaning: to pester or worry someone persistently

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to worry or harass; as a noun it is a broken-down horse.

clue.text: Aussie PM has well under half popular vote

indicators.note: the phrase contains the answer, and those four letters are far fewer than half of its eleven

explanation.surface: An Australian prime minister governs with far less than half the vote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aussie PM' looks like a prime minister, but PM is afternoon; Australians shorten afternoon to this.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian slang the afternoon, or post meridiem, is called the arvo.

clue.text: Worked together to hide damn portable radio!

indicators.note: to hide something is to enclose it, so the curse goes inside
worked means manipulated, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: blast! is a mild curse like damn!

explanation.surface: People cooperate to conceal a swear word, then exclaim about a radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worked' gives GHETTOER, which is split open to take the curse; the exclamation mark plays on the radio's loud volume.
explanation.definitionFit: A large portable stereo radio and cassette player was called a ghetto blaster in the 1980s.
